findings.source_passage: He looked so wistful as he went away, hearing the frolic, and evidently having none of his own.
findings.source_locator: After Mrs. March says she would have asked Laurie in if she'd known what was going on upstairs
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is the emotional keystone establishing Laurie's loneliness and isolation, which motivates Jo's determination to befriend him; its absence removes the affective grounding for one of the novel's central friendships.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim after Mrs. March's remark about asking him in: 'He looked so wistful as he went away, hearing the frolic, and evidently having none of his own.'

findings.source_passage: It's a mercy you didn't, mother! … But we'll have another play, some time, that he can see. Perhaps he'll help act; wouldn't that be jolly?
findings.source_locator: Immediately after Mrs. March's 'He looked so wistful' remark
findings.why_it_matters: This exchange is both voice-distinctive (Jo's exuberant projection of a shared future with Laurie) and a motif-initiating moment that plants the seed of the cross-fence friendship; its omission along with the wistful line above erases the Laurie-introduction payoff entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Jo's 'It's a mercy you didn't, mother!' exchange, ideally preceded by restoration of the 'so wistful' line that motivates it.

findings.source_passage: My mother knows old Mr. Laurence; but says he's very proud … Mother says he's very nice, though he never speaks to us girls.
findings.source_locator: The neighbor girl's speech at supper, between Jo's first mention of Laurie and Jo's cat-over-the-fence anecdote
findings.why_it_matters: This passage supplies the social-class and isolation context for Laurie's situation (proud grandfather, kept apart, tutor-bound) that makes his wistfulness legible; without it, the characterization of Laurie at chapter's end is thin and the neighbor-world texture is lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the neighbor girl's speech beginning 'My mother knows old Mr. Laurence' between Jo's first mention of Laurie being bashful and Jo's cat anecdote.

findings.source_passage: employed many hours which otherwise would have been idle, lonely, or spent in less profitable society.
findings.source_locator: After 'it was excellent drill for their memories, a harmless amusement'
findings.why_it_matters: The concluding clause of the narrator's aside is a period-register, morally evaluative voice marker; its removal flattens the narrator's characteristic didactic-ironic tone.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the full clause: '…employed many hours which otherwise would have been idle, lonely, or spent in less profitable society.'

summary: Three medium-severity losses—the 'wistful' Laurie characterization, Jo's follow-up 'help act' exchange, and the neighbor girl's contextualizing speech—collectively erase the chapter's carefully constructed Laurie introduction, which is interpretively foundational to the novel's central friendship arc.
